questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 48-year-old construction worker presented with complaints of unilateral loss of sweating on the face. He had a history of trauma to his back 1 month ago. Examination revealed the following findings. What is the likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Horner's or Bernard-Horner's syndrome. It can be caused by a lesion of the white ramus of T1. Horner's syndrome is characterized by a constricted pupil (miosis), drooping of the upper eyelid (ptosis), and absence of sweating of the face (anhidrosis), due to disruption of sympathetic nerve supply. In the autonomic nervous system, the sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral. The sympathetic chain receives white ramus inflow (preganglionic fibers) and gives gray ramus outflow (postganglionic fibers); white rami occur from T1-L2. In this setting sympathetic inflow at T1 is disrupted.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures of brachial plexus do not give branches?
questions.explanation: The divisions in the brachial plexus do not give any branches. The roots, trunks, and cords of the brachial plexus give direct branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements about brachial plexus is false?

options.text: Nerve to subclavius arises from superior trunk
Arterial supply to brachial plexus is from branches of common carotid arteries
Radial nerve is the largest branch of the entire brachial plexus
C4 contributes to brachial plexus occasionally

questions.correctAnswerText: Arterial supply to brachial plexus is from branches of common carotid arteries
questions.explanation: Arterial supply to the brachial plexus is from branches of the subclavian and vertebral arteries, not the common carotid arteries. The superior trunk gives the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6) and nerve to subclavius (C5, C6). The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the plexus and arises as a terminal branch of the posterior cord. Variations include a C4 pre-fixed plexus and T2 post-fixed plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An infraclavicular block was given in a patient with distal humerus fracture for open reduction and internal fixation. Which of the following branches of brachial plexus would likely be anesthetized?
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve would be anesthetized by an infraclavicular block because it is an infraclavicular branch arising from the posterior cord (C6-C8). Branches arising from roots and trunks are supraclavicular: dorsal scapular nerve (C5), long thoracic nerve of Bell, suprascapular nerve, and nerve to subclavius (C5, C6). Other branches arising from the cords are infraclavicular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A neonate is being examined after delivery. The delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia which led to the injury of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. Which of the following deformities is least likely to be seen in this neonate?

options.text: Abduction and medial rotation at shoulder joint
Sensory loss along the outer aspect of the arm

questions.correctAnswerText: Abduction and medial rotation at shoulder joint
questions.explanation: Upper trunk injury causes Erb or Erb-Duchenne palsy. It produces adduction and medial rotation at the shoulder, not abduction. The usual mechanism is excessive separation of head and neck, including birth injury, damaging C5-C6. Affected nerves include suprascapular, axillary, musculocutaneous, and radial nerves. The classic waiter's-tip posture includes arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, and sensory loss along the outer aspect of the arm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A medical student receives a booster dose of Hepatitis B vaccination. A few hours later, she develops weakness in the abduction and lateral rotation of that arm. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve, also called the surgeon's nerve, may be injured during inadvertent intramuscular injection. It is a branch of the posterior cord, exits the axilla through the quadrangular space, winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, and gives upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm supply over the lower deltoid. Injury can follow surgical-neck fracture, inferior shoulder dislocation, or IM injection and may cause regimental-badge anesthesia. Named nerves listed by the source: labourer's nerve = median nerve; musician's nerve = ulnar nerve; surgeon's nerve = axillary nerve; nerve of Bell = long thoracic nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nerves is not directly related to humerus?
questions.explanation: The median nerve is not directly related to the humerus. The axillary nerve is related to the surgical neck, the ulnar nerve to the medial epicondyle, and the radial nerve to the spiral/radial groove. The median nerve arises from lateral and medial cords, gives no muscular branch in the axilla and arm, supplies most superficial flexors in the forearm, passes between the two heads of pronator teres and gives the anterior interosseous nerve, gives a palmar cutaneous branch before the flexor retinaculum, and divides distally into recurrent and palmar digital branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following will you test in patients with median nerve injury at the wrist?

options.text: Loss of sensation of the palm
Loss of sensation on the ring finger

questions.explanation: Median nerve injury at the wrist is tested by contraction of abductor pollicis brevis; loss of thumb mobility/opposition can be tested by the pen test. Flexor pollicis brevis paralysis may occur with median nerve injury at the arm/elbow. Benediction-hand and Ochsner clasping tests are used for more proximal median lesions. The lateral half of the palm is supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch and is usually spared in carpal tunnel/wrist lesions because the branch does not pass through the carpal tunnel. Ring-finger sensation is not an isolated median-nerve test.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 56-year-old man presented with a loss of sensation over the hand as marked in the given image. Which of the following statements is true regarding the affected nerve?

options.text: It innervates medial half of flexor digitorum profundus
Ape thumb deformity can be seen irrespective of site of lesion
Wrist drop can be seen if the lesion is above the elbow

questions.correctAnswerText: Ape thumb deformity can be seen irrespective of site of lesion
questions.explanation: The marked sensory territory is supplied by the median nerve. Ape-thumb deformity is seen with median nerve lesions irrespective of site because it reflects distal denervation and non-use atrophy of the thenar muscles except adductor pollicis. The median nerve supplies the superficial flexor group except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus; its anterior interosseous branch supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and lateral half of FDP; recurrent branch supplies thenar muscles except adductor pollicis; palmar digital branches supply the lateral two lumbricals and skin of the lateral 3½ digits. Adductor pollicis and medial half of FDP are ulnar supplied, while wrist drop is a radial-nerve palsy.

questions.question: Lesion of the structure marked 'A' causes:

options.text: Loss of sensation of the nail of index finger
Loss of sensation at the tip of radial tubercle
Loss of sensation of the 4th interdigital cleft

questions.explanation: The structure marked A is the median nerve in the cubital fossa. Median nerve lesion causes loss of sensation of the nail of the index finger. questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following muscles are likely to be affected in patients with ulnar nerve injury at the elbow?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies the palmar interossei. It arises from the medial cord, supplies no muscle in the axilla or arm, runs medial to the brachial artery to mid-arm, then passes posteromedially through the medial intermuscular septum and arcade of Struthers. In the upper forearm it passes between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, gives a dorsal cutaneous branch distally, crosses the wrist superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's tunnel, and distal to the pisiform divides into superficial and deep terminal branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient came with complaints of inability to move his 4th and 5th digit, cannot hold a pen and he was not able to hold a paper between fingers. Which of the following sites given below is the probable cause of injury to the nerve in question?
questions.explanation: The presentation is of ulnar nerve injury; the most likely site shown is the medial epicondyle (marked C). Ulnar lesions may produce a positive card test, claw hand deformity, Froment's sign, Wartenberg sign, and palmaris brevis sign. A positive card test reflects weakness of palmar interossei and impaired finger adduction. questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is injured in a patient presenting with atrophy of hypothenar eminence and numbness in the palmar aspect of the little finger?

options.text: Ulnar nerve before its division into superficial and deep branch
Palmar cutaneous branch of ulnar nerve
Superficial terminal branch of ulnar nerve

questions.correctAnswerText: Ulnar nerve before its division into superficial and deep branch
questions.explanation: The findings indicate an ulnar nerve lesion before division into superficial and deep terminal branches because functions of both branches are affected. Distal to the pisiform, the superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis and skin of the palmar medial 1½ fingers; the deep branch runs with the deep palmar arch and supplies the intrinsic hand muscles except the first two lumbricals and thenar muscles. questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient is unable to hold a piece of paper between his thumb and index finger firmly following a cut wound over the hypothenar eminence. Which of the following nerves is likely to be damaged?

options.text: Superficial terminal branch of ulnar nerve

questions.explanation: Loss of thumb adduction points to injury of the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. The hypothenar wound can interrupt the branch before it reaches adductor pollicis. The deep branch initially supplies hypothenar muscles, then interossei and third/fourth lumbricals, and ends by supplying adductor pollicis and the medial/deep head of flexor pollicis brevis. It also sends articular filaments to the wrist joint.

questions.question: Which of the following digits can be used to test radial nerve, ulnar nerve, and median nerve?

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with paresthesias in the lower lateral part of the arm. Branch of which of the following nerve is affected here?
questions.explanation: The lower lateral part of the arm is supplied by the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, one of the radial-nerve branches arising in the spiral groove. The radial nerve is the largest brachial-plexus branch (C5-T1), leaves the axilla through the lower triangular space, travels in the radial groove with profunda brachii, and gives lower lateral cutaneous nerve of arm, posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm, branches to lateral and medial heads of triceps, and branch to anconeus. At the cubital fossa it divides into superficial sensory and deep motor branches; the deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve traverses supinator and supplies forearm extensors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient with radial head fracture presents with an inability to extend the metacarpophalangeal joint. On examination, wrist extension is normal with no sensory impairment. Which of the following is the probable cause?

options.text: Injury to the radial nerve just below the spiral groove
Injury to the anterior interosseous nerve
Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve
Injury to the common extensor origin

questions.correctAnswerText: Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve
questions.explanation: The presentation indicates posterior interosseous nerve injury. It is vulnerable in radial-head/neck fractures because the nerve winds around the radial neck into the posterior forearm. Lesions confined to the posterior interosseous nerve cause no cutaneous sensory loss. The deep radial branch supplies extensor carpi radialis brevis and supinator, then continues as the posterior interosseous nerve and passes near the supinator arch/arcade of Frohse.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the radial nerve is true?

options.text: It leaves the axilla by passing through the quadrangular space
Lateral head of triceps is paralyzed in a lesion of radial nerve in lower spiral groove
Anconeus is supplied by a branch arising in the axilla
In the arm it travels along the brachial artery

questions.correctAnswerText: Lateral head of triceps is paralyzed in a lesion of radial nerve in lower spiral groove
questions.explanation: The lateral head of triceps may be paralyzed in a lower radial-groove lesion because its branch arises in the lower spiral groove. Anconeus receives a branch from the spiral groove. The radial nerve is a posterior-cord branch, exits the axilla through the lower triangular space, and in the arm travels in the radial groove with the profunda brachii artery, not the brachial artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Pain and paresthesia are worse at night time
Paresthesia over the skin of thenar eminence is prominent
No artery passes through the tunnel

questions.correctAnswerText: Paresthesia over the skin of thenar eminence is prominent
questions.explanation: Paresthesia over the skin of the thenar eminence is not prominent in carpal tunnel syndrome because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve before it enters the tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome may result from reduced tunnel size, flexor-tendon synovial thickening/tenosynovitis, inflammation of the flexor retinaculum, or arthritic carpal changes including rheumatoid arthritis. Pain and paresthesia are often worse at night and with gripping. Contents include FDS, FDP and FPL tendons plus median nerve; no artery passes through the tunnel.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 13-year-old boy presents with injury to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Which of the following is least likely to be seen?

options.text: Weakness of the ulnar deviation and flexion
Complete paralysis of the IIIrd and IVth digits
Decreased sensation of the hypothenar eminence

questions.correctAnswerText: Complete paralysis of the IIIrd and IVth digits
questions.explanation: Medial epicondyle injury damages the ulnar nerve. Complete paralysis of the third and fourth digits is least likely because flexor digitorum superficialis (median nerve) and extensor digitorum (radial nerve) remain functional. Ulnar injury can weaken flexor carpi ulnaris causing reduced ulnar deviation/flexion, paralyze medial FDP, produce hypothenar atrophy, and reduce sensation over the medial hand/medial 1½ fingers.

questions.question: You are suspecting injury to the long thoracic nerve in a patient who underwent radical mastectomy. Which of the following tasks will you ask the patient to perform to test the integrity of the nerve?

Lift a heavy object from ground

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the deformity seen in patients with 'main en griffe'?

options.text: Extension at metacarpophalangeal joint and flexion at interphalangeal joint
Extension at both metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
Flexion at both metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
Flexion at metacarpophalangeal joint and extension at interphalangeal joint

questions.correctAnswerText: Extension at metacarpophalangeal joint and flexion at interphalangeal joint
questions.explanation: Main en griffe (claw hand) consists of extension/hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints due to ulnar nerve injury. The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, which normally flex MCP joints and extend IP joints. Loss of their action leaves extensor digitorum and long finger flexors unopposed.
